Camest
KAY-mest
v. (2nd pers. sing., past t.)
The second-person singular past of come, with the Old English -est ending. Webster 1828 lists it as the form used with thou. In John 16:30 it carries the disciples’ confession of the Lord’s pre-existence and mission, and in Genesis 16:8 it is the question the angel asks a runaway slave.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Camest appears at some of Scripture’s most searching moments, because to ask a person where he came from is to ask what he is doing. The angel of the LORD finds Hagar by a fountain in the wilderness and asks the two questions that expose her whole situation: Hagar, Sarai’s maid, whence camest thou? and whither wilt thou go? (Genesis 16:8). She can answer the first and not the second, which is the condition of every runaway. Eliab uses the form as a weapon against his younger brother: Why camest thou down hither? and with whom hast thou left those few sheep in the wilderness? (1 Samuel 17:28) — contempt disguised as concern for duty, spoken to the one man in the camp who was about to act. Ananias uses it to name the encounter on the Damascus road: the Lord, even Jesus, that appeared unto thee in the way as thou camest, hath sent me, that thou mightest receive thy sight (Acts 9:17), and the word brother that opens the sentence is one of the great small mercies of Scripture. Highest of all, the disciples use the form to confess the Lord’s origin: by this we believe that thou camest forth from God (John 16:30) — not that He was sent as prophets are sent, but that He came forth from the Father, which is the confession the whole Gospel of John is written to produce.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 gives CAMEST as the second person singular of the past tense of the verb come, used with thou: to move toward, to approach, to arrive, to proceed or issue from.

expand to see more

CAMEST — the second person singular, past tense, of the verb COME; used with the pronoun thou.

COME, v.i. — To move toward; to advance nearer, in any manner, and from any distance.

To arrive, as at some place or state; as, the letter is come; the time is come.

To proceed or issue from; as, wine comes from the grape; and in Scripture, to come forth from God.

From Saxon cuman, to come — the root also of became, welcome, and income.

Key Scripture

Genesis 16:8 — "And he said, Hagar, Sarai's maid, whence camest thou? and whither wilt thou go? And she said, I flee from the face of my mistress Sarai."

1 Samuel 17:28 — "And Eliab his eldest brother heard when he spake unto the men; and Eliab's anger was kindled against David, and he said, Why camest thou down hither? and with whom hast thou left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know thy pride, and the naughtiness of thine heart; for thou art come down that thou mightest see the battle."

Acts 9:17 — "And Ananias went his way, and entered into the house; and putting his hands on him said, Brother Saul, the Lord, even Jesus, that appeared unto thee in the way as thou camest, hath sent me, that thou mightest receive thy sight, and be filled with the Holy Ghost."

John 16:30 — "Now are we sure that thou knowest all things, and needest not that any man should ask thee: by this we believe that thou camest forth from God."

Modern Corruption

John 16:30 confesses that Christ came forth from God before He came into the world, and every adoptionist and merely-human account of Jesus — ancient Ebionite, Socinian, nineteenth-century liberal, or modern historical-Jesus reconstruction — must empty the verb of its origin.

expand to see more

To say that Christ came forth from God is to say He was with God before He came, and John states it flatly at the head of the Gospel: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The adoptionist alternative — that a man was raised to divine sonship at his baptism or resurrection — was condemned in the second century, revived by the Socinians, and is the working assumption of most reconstructions of a Jesus behind the Gospels. The dictionary names it as error rather than as an alternative reading. John 16:28 gives the full arc in the Lord’s own words: I came forth from the Father, and am come into the world: again, I leave the world, and go to the Father. A merely human Jesus has nowhere to come from and nowhere to return to.

Genesis 16:8 supplies the pastoral counterpart. God knows Hagar’s name, her station, and her mistress before He speaks, and He asks anyway, because the question is for her. She answers honestly about the flight and says nothing about the destination, since she had none. The Lord then sends her back to a hard house with a promise attached, and she names Him Thou God seest me. It is worth setting that against the modern counsel that would have confirmed her in the escape. Scripture’s mercy to the mistreated is real — the angel found her, not Sarai — but it does not consist in ratifying the flight; it consists in a promise large enough to make return bearable.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew bo (H935), to come, to go in, to enter; yatsa (H3318), to go out, to come forth; Greek erchomai (G2064), to come, to go; exerchomai (G1831), to come forth, to proceed out from.

expand to see more

Hebrew bo (H935) — to come in, to enter; used of Noah entering the ark and of the LORD coming to His temple.

Hebrew yatsa (H3318) — to go out, come forth; behind out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel (Micah 5:2).

Greek erchomai (G2064) — to come; the verb of the Lord’s advent and of His promised return.

Greek exerchomai (G1831) — to come forth out of; thou camest forth from God (John 16:30).

Greek heko (G2240) — to have come, to be present; Lo, I come: in the volume of the book it is written of me (Hebrews 10:7).

Usage

"Whence camest thou? and whither wilt thou go? (Genesis 16:8) — the two questions that expose a runaway."

"Why camest thou down hither? (1 Samuel 17:28) — contempt dressed as concern for duty."

"Thou camest forth from God (John 16:30) — the confession the Gospel of John was written to produce."
